clusters.name: Russell and Bettina's separation, 1987
clusters.reason: Around the time your father and stepmother separated over starting a family in 1987, three shifts pile up in the same months: you clashed with your stepfather and drew toward your dad, while your anxiety rose as you made the chess squad and found yourself out of your depth. Your stepmother's move out and later return, beside your own climb in that period, mark a time when the family's balance shifted around the question of another child.

clusters.name: Gordon's death, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Your grandfather Gordon died in June 1991 after years of kidney disease, and within the year around that time: your father's father came back into the family after years away in 1989, you began staying up late and your anxiety rose as you settled into secondary school in the rebuilt house in 1989, you dropped chess and joined the conservatory in 1991 where you leaned hard on your roommate Rafe, then injured your wrist and clashed with him as you spiralled into getting high and feeling lost and low. Your mother filled in your college forms and you let it happen. By 1992 your stepmother and father married in October. Your own shifts—the late nights, the injury, the blow-up with Rafe, dropping out—sit alongside your grandfather's death and your father's remarriage; your mother and stepmother's moves around the baby question years before had left their mark, and now the family was settling into a new shape with your grandfather gone and another child on the way.

clusters.name: Joelle's separation, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: In 1998 you bonded with Joelle, and within months in 1999 two shifts pile up around your split: your insomnia worsened and your anxiety rose before concerts though you were playing the best you ever had and winning competitions. You separated in July 1999 and started with a therapist in August. Your own trouble—the sleeplessness and the split—sits here with no one else's shifts beside it, so this period holds only your own story.

clusters.name: Winifred's cancer, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Your grandmother Winifred was found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, around the same time you began running out of steam for performing and your anxiety rose. You had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in early 2002 and were done with performing. By September 2002 you were on poor terms with family and friends and left Thornbury for Gull Harbour. You met Marisol at a winter party in 2003, moved to Fenwick to live with her, then separated within the year and sank into a deep depression once you were back in Thornbury that winter. You avoided your family—could not face them—but relied, gingerly, on friends: Corbin, Dale, and Silas. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home and died in February 2004. Within those same months you requested help from your parents with therapy costs and returned to your therapist Victor. The shifts in your own functioning and your distance from family pile up around your grandmother's illness and death, your own burnout, and the failed relationship; the depression that followed the split with Marisol took months to lift, and you drew toward friends rather than toward your parents through it all.

clusters.name: Lorna's death, 2008
clusters.reason: Your grandmother Lorna died in January 2008, and within months around that time: you spent four weeks building at Alder Creek with Silas before nursing school. Your mother pressed you to visit, driving out regardless when you said the timing was wrong, and you kept the door shut on her. When you left for nursing school in Marlow Sound in September 2008, you stopped speaking to your mother; the silence held for roughly a year. Within the same months, your aunt Imogen had a stroke in January 2009 and spent months in rehabilitation. Your distance from your mother piles up around your grandmother's death and your own move away for nursing school; the lodge visit with your mother went wrong, and afterward every call cost too much.

clusters.name: Wren's arrival and integration, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: You married Wren in March 2017, and over the next two years multiple shifts pile up: your contact with your mother eased off slightly once Wren came along. Your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in October 2017. By late 2019 you saw your mother less, aiming for shorter regular calls instead. That same October your sister Tara was expecting her first child, your father's first grandchild. Late October 2019 brought a street party, a fundraising dinner, and a drive to the lake for Wren's mother's retirement: Wren became swamped by it all, her anxiety and symptoms rose and her functioning fell. You overfunctioned, laying out a plan to settle her. Wren's family—her father, brother, and their children—are fused; they talk all day and nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. At the lake weekend you were awake from the small hours, could not sleep, and pulled back as the others rose; your sleep is at its worst around her family, and you feel you don't belong. Wren was anxious after your sleepless nights at family occasions. The period holds shifts across you, Wren, and her family around the integration of the two households and Wren's family's intensity.
